titre: The Church Withdraws Its Priests, and Proof Has to Be Invented
accroche: In 1215, a council forbids clerics to take part in ordeals. With no divine judge, Europe must find who will establish the facts.
contenu_vulgarise:
For centuries, much of Europe settled its hardest trials by entrusting them to God. The accused grasped a red-hot iron or plunged an arm into boiling water. Three days later, the bandaged hand was examined: healed, it declared innocence; infected, guilt. These trials are called ordeals, and they should be seen less as barbarism than as an answer to a practical problem. When a fact can be established neither by confession nor by witness, some procedure is needed to get out of the impasse, and this one had the advantage of being accepted by all.

## The link the council removes

The priest's role was not decorative: the cooperation of clerics was part of the ordeal, and it is what gave it its religious warrant. Without it, the ordeal was nothing but a burn.

In November 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council, meeting in Rome under Innocent III, forbids clerics to lend their ministry to these trials. The provision does not condemn ordeals in a grand speech; it simply withdraws the priest. Deprived of its warrant, the practice recedes. In England, the court rolls contain no ordeal after 1219, when Henry III acknowledges their abolition; elsewhere in Europe, it grows rarer through the late Middle Ages and does not disappear entirely until the 16th century.

The courts of Europe then face a void, and the most concrete question there is. A man is accused, he denies it, there is no confession and no decisive witness: who decides, and how?

## Two answers, two legal families

In England, procedure relies on a group of neighborhood men brought together to say what they hold to be true. The jury had already existed for about forty years as an instrument of inquiry: the ban on ordeals puts it in a position to establish guilt. The judge states the law, jurors say what happened.

On the Continent, the Church courts move toward the other path. The judge himself conducts the inquiry. This is the so-called inquisitorial procedure, which the council of 1215 confirms for Church courts, while the English common law courts keep an adversarial system.

It is not the only cause of the split between the two great families of Western law, the common law family and the written-law systems of the Continent, but it has its share in it. They differ not first by their codes or their courts, but by what they put in God's place when He had to be replaced, and by whom they charged with saying what really happened.

The questions asked in 1215 have not aged: to whom do we entrust the establishing of the facts, and must that person explain the decision?

repere.texte: In November 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council forbids clerics to take part in ordeals. In England, the court rolls contain none after 1219; elsewhere, they grow rarer through the late Middle Ages and survive into the 16th century.

carte.punch: By removing the priest from the ordeal, a council forced Europe to rethink proof.
carte.idee: In 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council forbids clerics to take part in ordeals. Without a divine guarantor, someone has to decide who establishes the facts: the jury in England, the judge's inquiry on the Continent. Two legal families find one of their roots here.

quiz.question: How did the 1215 council's decision make ordeals disappear?
choix: By forbidding clerics to take part, when their cooperation was part of the procedure
By expressly condemning them as a superstition contrary to Christian doctrine
By requiring courts to rely henceforth on the testimony of jurors
By providing for the excommunication of judges who continued to use them
quiz.explication: The council did not prohibit the ordeal itself; it forbade clerics to take part. Without that cooperation, the ordeal lost its religious warrant, and the practice receded, in England as early as 1219, more slowly elsewhere.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under which pope was the Fourth Lateran Council, which forbade clerics to take part in ordeals, held?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry places the council in November 1215, in Rome, under Innocent III.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year do the English court rolls stop containing ordeals, when Henry III acknowledges their abolition?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the English rolls contain no ordeal after 1219, four years after the council.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, who establishes the facts in England once ordeals are withdrawn?
choix: A group of neighborhood men, the jury
The judge alone, through his own inquiry
A judicial duel between the parties
The priest, through a new trial
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In England, a group of neighborhood men says what it holds to be true; on the Continent, it is the judge who conducts the inquiry.
